analysis.one_liner: Gives people the right to have websites delete personal data collected about them as children.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced by Sen. Durbin with 3 Democratic cosponsors in April 2021, never received a committee hearing or vote and died when the 117th Congress ended in January 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would amend the 1998 Children's Online Privacy Protection Act so that anyone over 13 could ask a website or online service aimed at children to permanently delete all personal information collected from or about them before they turned 13. Websites would have to post clear instructions for making such a request, delete the data promptly, and confirm the deletion in writing, with narrow exceptions for court cases and law enforcement. The Federal Trade Commission would write the rules within a year, and state attorneys general could enforce the law too.
analysis.who_benefits: Anyone whose childhood data now sits in a company's files: people who used child-oriented websites, apps, games, or online services before turning 13. The bill lets them or their guardian wipe that record — including data their parents consented to sharing years earlier — so it cannot be used for advertising, profiling, or resale.
analysis.who_benefits_short: People whose childhood data companies hold

how_it_helps.text: Creates a legal right to deletion of personal information collected from or about a person before age 13, even when parental consent was given at the time [S3].
Requires covered websites to prominently explain how to request deletion, delete the data promptly, and send written confirmation [S2][S3].
Defines deletion as true removal — the information must no longer be retrievable in the normal course of business, not just hidden from view [S3].
Gives the FTC one year to write the rules and lets state attorneys general enforce the new requirement, adding a second layer of oversight [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Operators of child-directed websites and online services — from large platforms to small kids' game and education sites — would bear the cost of building deletion systems, honoring requests, and confirming completion, plus FTC or state enforcement risk if they fail.
analysis.who_pays_short: Websites and services aimed at children

drawbacks.text: Compliance is a real cost: covered operators would have to build systems to locate, purge, and confirm deletion of years-old childhood records, a heavier lift for small children's sites than for large platforms [S3].

The right is narrow: it covers only websites and services directed to children (or operators who knowingly collected from a child), not the much larger stock of childhood data held by general-audience platforms and data brokers [S2][S3].

Identity verification is a practical hurdle — the bill requires a request from the individual or guardian 'acting with the knowledge and consent' of the individual but leaves the FTC to work out how operators confirm who is asking, raising fraud and privacy questions [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is a genuine, permanent privacy right for a specific group — people whose data was collected as children — and the exceptions for courts and law enforcement are sensible. The costs are modest compliance burdens on child-focused websites, and the main limitation is the bill's narrow scope: it would not touch the far larger volume of childhood data held by general platforms. A reasonably designed, incremental measure.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and referred to the Senate Commerce Committee in April 2021, and the committee never acted on it before the Congress ended in January 2023.

narrative.text: Sen. Durbin introduced the bill on April 28, 2021, joined by Sens. Markey, Blumenthal, and Hirono as original cosponsors [S3][S4].
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation the same day; that is the last action of any kind in its record [S5].
The committee never held a markup, reported the bill, or sent it to the floor, and the bill died when the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023 [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Operators of child-directed websites and online services keep childhood data indefinitely with no deletion obligation, and no one else gains from the bill's failure.

for.name: Sen. Richard Durbin
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to amend COPPA with a childhood-data deletion right.

for.name: Sens. Ed Markey, Richard Blumenthal, and Mazie Hirono
for.what_they_did: Joined as original cosponsors at introduction; the bill drew no other cosponsors in two years.

against.name: Sen. Maria Cantwell
against.role: Chair, Senate Commerce, Science, and Transportation Committee
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill; it sat in committee until the Congress expired.

sides.party_line_note: All four sponsors were Democrats and no Republican ever cosponsored or publicly opposed the bill on the record; there was no vote, so no partisan split can be measured.

industries.industry: Child-directed websites and online services (kids' games, apps, and platforms)
industries.note: These companies would lose the ability to hold childhood data indefinitely and would bear the cost of deletion systems and confirmation duties. Their interest in keeping the data — the raw material for advertising and profiling — runs against the person whose data it is.
Data collected from children feeds advertising profiles and downstream brokers; a deletion right shrinks that supply. No industry group appears on the record for or against the bill.
